title: SpaceX vs. Nvidia: The Best AI Stock to Buy Now - The Motley Fool
content: SpaceX's latest results have investors reconsidering the top AI stock. Few companies are more synonymous with artificial intelligence (AI) investing than Nvidia (NVDA -0.80%). It's been the leader in AI investing since the AI build-out kicked off in 2023, and nothing has changed since. However, there are many new investment options in the AI world, including Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -0.92%). SpaceX has a major AI wing thanks to its acquisition of xAI before going public, and this division has delivered incredible growth. In fact, it has some investors wondering if it's one of the best AI investments on the market right now. But is it better than Nvidia? One thing to note is that Nvidia and SpaceX aren't competitors; they're partners. Nvidia makes graphics processing units (GPUs), which are broad-purpose computing units that excel in nearly any environment. This makes them extremely flexible, and with Nvidia's GPUs being recognized as the best available, they're quite popular. In fact, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that Nvidia's new Vera Rubin architecture is the best available and that SpaceX will exclusively deploy Nvidia's products for its AI endeavors. That's a pretty notable endorsement, and it solidifies the relationship between these two. SpaceX's AI product centers around its Grok large language model. This has become a popular model to use because it's connected to X, which helps it understand current events. It also offers other products like Grok Bots, which are becoming popular because they give users access to AI agents that can handle tasks on their behalf. Nvidia and SpaceX are two distinct investments, as Nvidia is on the infrastructure side, and SpaceX is on the application side. Although there's still a lot of AI computing infrastructure to build, companies are starting to move into the application phase of AI, which may favor SpaceX delivering better results. That's exactly what we're seeing now, as SpaceX just blew expectations out of the water in the third quarter. During Q3, SpaceX's Super Intelligence (SI) division (the new name of its AI division) saw revenue increase at a jaw-dropping 830% rate. While this quarter's results included an acquisition that boosted the segment's overall growth rate, it was still a monster quarter for SpaceX. In fact, it topped anything that Nvidia has ever delivered during the AI build-out. NVDA Revenue (Quarterly YOY Growth) data by YCharts. While Nvidia's most recent 106% growth rate is still very impressive and nothing to complain about, it just isn't growing nearly as fast as SpaceX. However, there is one huge difference. SpaceX is more focused on capturing market share, so it doesn't care a lot about profitability. Still, its operating income for its AI division was $431 million on revenue of $7.56 billion, good for a 5.7% margin. On the flip side, Nvidia's operating margin for its most recent quarter was 66%. This means that Nvidia is producing huge profits while SpaceX's are comparatively minimal. That should be expected based on the phase each company is in. Still, the speed at which Nvidia is already growing, combined with incredible profitability, causes me to prefer Nvidia's financial picture. Because SpaceX is barely profitable, I think valuing it based on expected sales this year makes the most sense. Right now, SpaceX has a market cap of $2 trillion, and Wall Street expects 2026 revenue of $48.6 billion. That equates to a forward price-to-sales ratio of about 41. Nvidia is expected to generate $411.7 billion in revenue this year. With a market cap of $5.1 trillion, Nvidia's stock is priced at just 12 times sales. So, Nvidia is about three times cheaper than SpaceX on that measure, which I think solidifies Nvidia as the best AI stock to invest in right now. While SpaceX could still be a solid AI choice, Nvidia is a far safer and more surefire pick. Keithen Drury has positions in Nvidia. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nvidia. Nvidia's (NVDA) business is booming, but one sector of the market remains a seemingly impenetrable morass for the world's leading chip designer: China. For years, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has struggled to gain a foothold in the world's second-largest economy, due in large part to restrictions imposed by the Department of Commerce, which regulates international chip sales. Seeking inroads, Huang has repeatedly urged the White House to loosen those restrictions, which the administration says are necessary for national security and for the US to remain ahead in the AI race. When Nvidia last reported earnings, forward guidance once again omitted sales projections for China, continually snarled by state politics. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. The complicated relationship between Nvidia and China was thrust back into public light on Thursday after the New York Times reported new US intelligence efforts. The US intelligence service, the report says, believes a Chinese national named Alice Huang — who has served as a leader of Nvidia chip customer Megaspeed and who maintains a well-documented relationship with Huang himself — has acted as an intelligence asset and passed information to the governing party in Beijing. The reporting raises major questions about potential information leakage from Nvidia to China, not only regarding trade secrets but also about Jensen Huang's increasingly deep ties to the White House as he has lobbied for eased restrictions. At the All-In summit in September, Huang took a call from Trump on stage, putting the US leader on speakerphone as Trump dismissed fears around AI's security implications as a "scam." The race between the US and China to develop and disseminate their own AI technology has, over the past several years, become a paramount concern for the leadership of both governments. While China has matched or even surpassed the US on the development and distribution of "open weight" AI models, which often come at far cheaper costs than "closed weight" alternatives, the US frontier labs such as Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) have retained the lead in developing the most advanced models. Powering those advanced models are chips designed by Nvidia, whose leading semiconductors are often regarded as the gold standard for computing performance. While the chips are hugely popular in the US and other global markets, the Commerce Department has, since 2022, blocked Nvidia from selling successive generations of its chips to Chinese buyers as Washington seeks to maintain its edge over Beijing. Huang won a victory for his company in December 2025 when he secured permission from the Trump administration for Nvidia to export some H200 chips to Chinese buyers, a policy change that came amid a $5 million lobbying push by Nvidia throughout the year. Even chip models such as the H200, which are now several generations behind Nvidia's flagship products, remain competitive for Chinese buyers with options available from companies like Huawei Technologies. Yet H200 sales accounted for less than 1% of Nvidia's $89 billion in data center revenue for the second quarter, Nvidia said. Part of that dearth in sales has also come from Beijing, which recently moved to block Chinese buyers from purchasing Nvidia chips as Xi Jinping's government looks to reduce dependence on US technology, instead turning to homegrown alternatives from the likes of Huawei. Given the "ongoing geopolitical uncertainty," Nvidia CFO Colette Kress told analysts, "there is no China data center compute revenue in our forward outlook." While it's not clear how many H200 chips Nvidia sold to Chinese buyers in the second quarter, those sales fell below the US-approved maximum due to blocks imposed by the Chinese government, the company said. "Under the current rules and geopolitical landscape, we are unable to create and deliver a competitive product for wide distribution in China's data center market with the approval from both the USG and the Chinese government," Nvidia said in its second quarter earnings report. The restrictions haven't stopped Chinese buyers from pursuing workarounds to obtain some of the world's leading chips. Since the US government imposed its sales restrictions on Nvidia, a black-market shadow trade has sprung up in response, according to public reporting and investigations by the Department of Justice. Buyers and sellers throughout Southeast Asian nations not under restrictions import chips under legitimate guises, then switch labels, change packaging, or use other methods to disguise the package's true contents before sending the chips onward into China, reporting and the US government have alleged. Inside China, users on Douyin, the nation's version of TikTok, openly hawk sanctioned chips such as Nvidia's Blackwell B300, priced at millions of US dollars per server, in videos reviewed by Yahoo Finance. Such sales would likely contravene the Commerce Department's restrictions. Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company that employed Alice Huang, has been investigated by US authorities for more than a year due to concerns that the company may be sending Nvidia's most advanced chips to data centers throughout Southeast Asia that serve Chinese companies or directly funneling the physical chips into China through intermediaries, per the New York Times. Nvidia has repeatedly stated that there's no evidence its chips are being smuggled into China, and the company said to the New York Times that if someone close to the company were a "threat to American industry," Nvidia is confident the US government would make the company aware. The company added that while Huang often talks with customers, those conversations never include "information relevant to national security." Even so, for Huang and Nvidia, the headlines come as a reminder of the geopolitical tensions inherent to the AI trade. While it's in Nvidia's interest to serve as wide a customer base as possible, national security concerns in Washington continue to interfere with the company's ability to sell into the world's second-largest economy, where buyers have shown willingness to pay top dollar for its products. title: NVDA's Gross Margin Faces Pressure: Can It Offset Rising Memory Costs? - The Globe and Mail
content: NVIDIA Corporation’s NVDA gross margins could face pressure as rising memory costs and supply constraints challenge its ability to maintain strong profitability. However, the company’s pricing power, growing AI demand and shift toward advanced platforms could help offset some of these headwinds. Still, NVIDIA expects gross margin to decline sequentially to 74% in the third quarter of fiscal 2027, plus or minus 50 basis points. Higher memory prices are a key concern because advanced AI systems require large amounts of high-performance memory. Tight supply could increase component costs and limit production flexibility. NVIDIA has several ways to protect profitability. Its strong relationships with major memory suppliers could help secure supplies, while its advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) and integrated computing systems give it pricing power. The company is also increasing supply and capacity commitments to support future demand. The Vera Rubin platform offers another potential boost. Its improved computing performance and efficiency could help customers justify higher spending on AI infrastructure, supporting NVIDIA’s ability to pass on some cost increases. Overall, NVIDIA’s margins may face near-term pressure, but strong demand and pricing power provide important support. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.AMD and Intel CorporationINTC are expanding their AI businesses, but rising component costs and production challenges could affect their profitability. However, Advanced Micro Devices’ third-quarter guidance indicates gross margin will remain flat sequentially. Intel’s second-quarter revenues increased 25% to $16.1 billion, while its non-GAAP gross margin improved to 41.8% from 29.7% a year earlier. Still, Intel warned that shortages of memory, substrates and other components could persist into 2027, potentially limiting shipments and increasing costs. Both companies face cost and supply challenges as AI infrastructure demand grows. NVIDIA has an advantage, with a 75% gross margin in fiscal second-quarter 2027, although its margin is expected to decline sequentially to 74% in the third quarter. title: Nvidia Shareholders Have a Major Reason to Be Bullish After Jensen Huang's Latest Announcement - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia's evolution into a full-stack AI hardware provider comes with big opportunities. Nvidia's (NVDA -0.80%) GTC Conference in Berlin ran from Oct. 20 through Oct. 22, and CEO Jensen Huang shared some interesting insights into the evolution of the artificial intelligence (AI) market. In addition to expounding on the importance of AI technologies for European countries and companies, Huang detailed the significance of new technologies from his company. Huang's keynote at the GTC event focused heavily on data centers transitioning into "AI factories" -- and he highlighted a new Nvidia product that's set to be central to the transformation. Here's why Nvidia's recent shifts in approach to the AI data center market look like a bullish development for shareholders. Huang used the occasion of GTC to spotlight Nvidia's new comprehensive server racks and their ability to deliver full AI factory performance. The product combines 72 of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs) with 256 new custom language processing unit chips. Crucially, the servers aren't just built around its Vera Rubin graphics processing units -- they also include the company's Vera family central processing units (CPUs). Through the integration of the company's CPUs and other hardware, Nvidia sees its monetization of AI compute applications broadening substantially. During the company's recent quarterly call, management said that its sales opportunity per gigawatt of compute has expanded from $18 billion with Hopper to $25 billion with Blackwell to $40 billion with the Vera Rubin family. The big increase in expected sales per gigawatt of compute is being aided substantially by Nvidia's CPU integrations, and the company expects that the increasing importance of AI inference will power new market share gains. While advanced GPUs are the crucial hardware for training advanced AI models, high-performance CPUs can often carry out the inference processes needed to actually run the models in ways that are more efficient in terms of hardware and energy costs. Speaking on the company's new comprehensive server rack product at the company's previous GTC event in March, Huang said, "This is the AI future. This is where AI wants to go. It's designed for inference, this one workload. And this workload is what drives AI factories." At the more recent GTC event in Berlin, Huang said that a 1-gigawatt AI factory would cost operators about $50 billion to set up. Meanwhile, he estimates that such a facility would generate roughly $40 billion in annual revenue, and that delaying bringing the AI factory online by just three months would result in the loss of $10 billion in potential sales. The risk of missing out on tech breakthroughs and revenue has been central to the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure, and it does appear to be a meaningful one. Recent concerns about a valuation bubble in the AI space have created volatility for many stocks in the category, but Huang is highlighting a dynamic that could see players left behind if they don't spend sufficiently on AI compute capabilities. title: NVDA Stock Retreats as Google TPUs and Nvidia Debt Risk Challenge the Growth Outlook - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia stock retreated after rebounding, with resistance at $220 as Google’s expanding TPU business, rising financing costs and data-centre power shortages raise questions about the sustainability of semiconductor demand. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares recovered towards $220 after falling to $210 last Friday, but the rebound has struggled to gain traction following an earlier retreat from record highs above $243. The stock is pulling back again despite improving sentiment across parts of the semiconductor sector, as investors reassess the costs and risks associated with expanding computing infrastructure. Expectations of persistent memory shortages and higher prices have supported chipmakers, but strong demand alone may not guarantee continued growth. Nvidia’s customers must secure sufficient financing, electricity and operational capacity to deploy increasingly expensive processors. The central concern is whether technology companies can convert substantial infrastructure commitments into profitable services before rising costs and competitive pressures undermine returns. Google’s expanding custom-chip business presents another challenge. On Tuesday, Google and Oracle announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. The agreement marks the first time Google’s TPUs will be offered through another hyperscale cloud platform. The arrangement could give Oracle customers an alternative to Nvidia-powered computing systems, particularly for workloads suited to Google’s specialised processors. Nvidia retains significant advantages through its established software ecosystem, broad customer base and high-performance GPU platform. However, Google’s move demonstrates how major technology companies are seeking greater flexibility over computing costs and hardware supply. If custom chips become increasingly competitive, Nvidia could face pressure on pricing and market share in selected applications, even if overall computing demand continues to grow. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that planned semiconductor manufacturing capacity in 2027 and 2028 might not fully meet anticipated demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Its US-listed shares reportedly fell approximately 4%, adding pressure to semiconductor stocks. Manufacturing constraints could support chip prices, but they may also delay the equipment required to expand production. For Nvidia, supply limitations can complicate customers’ deployment schedules and restrict how quickly additional computing capacity becomes operational. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $210 again last week but we’re seeing some improvement this week until today. Financing conditions are another concern. Such elevated borrowing costs illustrate the risks of funding capital-intensive data-centre projects through debt. If financing becomes more expensive, operators may postpone projects, reduce expansion plans or demand stronger evidence of future profitability. These pressures could eventually affect Nvidia’s order growth if customers become more selective about new commitments. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) reportedly faces another infrastructure bottleneck: insufficient electricity at some data centres. According to Business Insider, certain server racks containing Nvidia hardware have remained in warehouses while facilities await the capacity needed to operate them. Amazon reportedly expected to receive $5 billion in Nvidia server systems in August, followed by another $3 billion monthly. Its Early Rack Receipt programme allows it to secure equipment before facilities are ready for deployment. Securing hardware in advance may help Amazon manage equipment shortages, but it also creates potential storage costs and delays between delivery and commercial use. For Nvidia, the distinction between orders and productive deployment is important. Customers may continue purchasing processors in the near term, but prolonged power shortages could delay returns and influence future spending decisions. Questions surrounding OpenAI’s revenue have also renewed scrutiny of infrastructure investment. Its annualised revenue run rate was reportedly around $50 billion at the end of September, below the widely circulated $68 billion figure, which reportedly included partner-generated revenue. The distinction highlights the need to assess whether demand for computing services can support the enormous costs of infrastructure expansion. If revenue growth fails to keep pace with capital expenditure, major technology companies could reconsider their spending plans. Meanwhile, expectations of worsening memory shortages in 2027 have supported semiconductor sentiment. However, higher memory prices could also increase data-centre costs, adding further pressure to already substantial infrastructure budgets. Nvidia remains well positioned to benefit from demand for advanced processors, but competition, financing costs, manufacturing constraints and electricity shortages are becoming harder to ignore. A sustained recovery above $220 would help improve the near-term technical picture, although the stock remains below its earlier record highs. If infrastructure spending slows or customers struggle to deploy purchased hardware, the shares could face renewed selling pressure. The key question is no longer simply how many processors Nvidia can sell, but whether its customers can finance, power and profitably operate the infrastructure required to justify continued expansion.

Nvidia invented the GPU, the chip behind nearly every major AI system on the planet. But it’s so much more today. It sells entire “AI factories” in a box: multi-rack systems packed with processors, memory, servers, cooling, and the high-speed networking that lets everything work together like one big “brain.” And its CUDA software is so deeply embedded across every cloud, AI lab, and frontier model that it’s become the de facto AI infrastructure operating system. Nvidia grew revenue 106% year over year from $46.7 billion to $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027 (ended July 26, 2026). That’s unprecedented. No public company in history has ever organically doubled quarterly revenue from such a large base. Nvidia’s “Data Center” revenue, which is the AI business, grew 117% year over year in Q2 to $89 billion. The company guided for total revenue of $108 billion this quarter, which would be its first $100 billion quarter. It also guided for 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, which is basically calendar year 2027. And the cap on that growth guidance is supply, not demand. The company said it would have been about double again absent the supply crunch. Meanwhile, the customer list has broadened considerably. For two years, the most popular argument against Nvidia was basically: “Its whole business depends on four giant customers, all of which are building their own chips to become less reliant on Nvidia.” It’s true that these four “hyperscalers”—Amazon, Microsoft, Google (GOOGL), and Meta Platforms (META)—have been driving much of the AI infrastructure buildout. They’ll continue to do so for at least a few more years. And all four are indeed building their own AI chips these days. But as the hyperscalers have increased their AI spending, so have lots of other companies. Governments around the world have too for their “sovereign AI” initiatives. And we now have a lot more color on that broadening AI spending… In Q1, Nvidia started separating its AI revenue into two buckets. Bucket one is the hyperscalers. Bucket two is everybody else, which Nvidia calls ACIE (short for AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise). So ACIE covers the neoclouds, governments, hospitals, banks, carmakers, drug companies, AI startups, etc. Meanwhile, most of the customers in the faster-growing ACIE bucket will never even think about designing their own chips. What’s more, the hyperscalers have shown no signs of pulling back yet. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said it clearly on the call: “With cloud industry backlog now greater than $2 trillion, CapEx by the top five hyperscalers is expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.” (Oracle is the fifth hyperscaler she referred to.) And Amazon—which does design its own AI chips and has basically been Exhibit A for the whole “hyperscalers will defect” thesis—committed to deploying another 2 million Nvidia GPUs through 2028. Amazon is also adopting Nvidia’s full physical AI stack (Omniverse, Cosmos, Isaac, and Jetson) to power its fleet of warehouse robots. So the giants are still buying from Nvidia, a new class of customer has shown up behind them, and both are compounding at once. First, the Vera Rubin ramp. Nvidia expects supply to stay tight through at least fiscal 2028 (basically calendar 2027). We want to see the company deliver at least the 70% growth it expects. I also want gross margin to bottom in the 71% to 72% range. If it falls below that threshold, it means memory costs are temporarily winning the tug-of-war Second, how much Nvidia invests in, guarantees, and backstops its customers. It has about $165 billion in these types of financing arrangements. Critics call this “circular financing.” But we’re not concerned. Those guarantees are only about 1.3X Nvidia’s trailing 12-month free cash flow… and only about half of our two-year forward annual free cash flow forecast. What’s more, if a customer fails, what’s left behind is Nvidia equipment that other buyers are lining up for, not dark fiber like after the dot-com bust. Third, the Open Agent Safety Platform Nvidia launched just this week. It’s a two-piece (hardware and software) system for keeping AI agents inside the boundaries set by operators. The launch follows disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google of recent incidents in which their AI models escaped their test sandboxes—during testing with safeguards reduced, I should add—and hacked other organizations. Nvidia says that from what it knows about the most notorious of such incidents—OpenAI’s models breaching Hugging Face—this new platform could have stopped it. The significance: Nvidia is basically trying to make its hardware the place where AI agent safety lives. And it’s giving away the software layer to make that architecture the industry default—the classic CUDA-style playbook applied to safety. It strengthens the “you need the whole Nvidia stack” narrative and gives CEO Jensen Huang a powerful talking point and a place at the table on one of the industry’s biggest problems. But it’s effectively an “option” on the future, not a moat today. And the open design means the door is deliberately left open for others. P.S. content: Shares of Nvidia Corp (NVDA) slipped 1% on Wednesday  following reports that the U.S. Department of Justice has inquired about how its planned acquisition of Hugging Face could affect competition in artificial intelligence. According to a report from Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter, department officials have asked whether the Hugging Face deal would allow Nvidia to control a key distribution point for AI models and tools. The questioning adds to the years-long probe by antitrust regulators on Nvidia’s conduct, which kicked off under former President Joe Biden, the report said. The probe is reportedly continuing with no indication that current President Donald Trump has any involvement. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a relationship with Trump and recently joined the President on his diplomatic trip to China. The DOJ’s recent line of questioning covers the company’s acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether it has pressured customers, sources told Reuters. As part of the probe, the DOJ has reportedly examined Nvidia’s other acquisition deals, including the December 2025 deal to buy SchedMD, sources told Reuters. The department has also scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its licensing deal with chip startup Groq and its acquisition of Run.ai, the report added. Nvidia announced in early September that it had agreed to buy Hugging Face for approximately $12.93 billion. The transaction includes roughly $11.9 billion payable to Hugging Face’s investors and an equity-based retention program of up to about $1 billion for employees who join Nvidia. Hugging Face operates a widely used platform that hosts millions of open-source AI models, datasets, and applications, serving millions of developers and hundreds of thousands of companies. It is often described as a central hub for open AI development. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pledged that the platform will remain open to models, frameworks, clouds, and computing platforms from across the industry, and that Nvidia’s own chips will not be required to use it. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. With a market cap of about $5.3 trillion, Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the largest company in the world -- and it's easy to see how it reached that size. The tech giant's advanced processors are the dominant compute hardware in the data centers that underpin the entire generative artificial intelligence (AI) industry, and as soaring demand for its chips continues to outstrip supply, it enjoys booming sales at sky-high margins. That said, all investors know that past performance doesn't guarantee future results. And the larger a company becomes, the harder it is for additional growth to move the needle on its finances. So what might this leading tech stock be worth by the end of 2027? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » It's been roughly four years since OpenAI's ChatGPT introduced the world to the power of generative AI, and the revolution that it triggered shows no signs of slowing down. According to analysts at Goldman Sachs, tech companies' AI-related capital expenditures will total more than $1 trillion in 2026. And much of that spending will go toward graphics processing units (GPUs) and other data center compute hardware created by companies like Nvidia. The supply of advanced semiconductor equipment remains tight relative to demand, and Nvidia's GPUs remain the most popular data center AI accelerators, a situation that allows it to charge high prices. These persistent tailwinds were reflected in the company's second-quarter earnings. Revenue jumped 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, driven mostly by strength in the company's data center segment, which grew 117%. This business involves designing and selling advanced AI infrastructure. And management plans to keep the momentum going with new releases, such as its Vera Rubin platform, which is designed specifically to handle agentic AI workloads. Nvidia's bottom line is also looking good; the company's net income jumped 32% year over year to $59.7 billion in the period. On the surface, Nvidia looks like the perfect stock to own. But investors should be aware that it faces some big challenges. Perhaps the biggest is its lack of diversification. In the past, Nvidia boasted a broader business model as it sold GPUs for consumer video games, machine learning, cryptocurrency mining, virtual reality devices, and data centers, among other uses. However, the mix of end-uses has condensed dramatically: Data centers now account for over 90% of its revenue. This situation leaves Nvidia exceptionally exposed to a potential downturn in the AI market. And even the bulls should be willing to accept that the current levels of data center spending probably won't last forever. A recent paper by Columbia University finance professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh (first presented at the nonpartisan Brookings Institution) concludes that U.S. businesses and consumers will eventually have to spend the equivalent of 9% of the country's GDP on AI-related services to justify the current levels of capital investment going toward the technology. That's as much as we spend on food, and far more than we spend on essentials like energy and construction. While large language models (LLMs) are useful, they are notoriously difficult to monetize due to their huge energy consumption and the intense level of competition in the space, especially from lower-cost Chinese alternatives. In fact, industry leader Anthropic reported an eye-popping net loss of $80 billion in the first half of 2026. If the consumer-facing side of the AI market struggles to turn a profit, that could eventually lead to a smaller market for hardware providers like Nvidia. Trading today at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 23.5, Nvidia stock is still relatively cheap relative to its growth potential. And investors who believe the AI boom will maintain its momentum can comfortably expect the stock to offer additional multibagger returns from here. That said, this represents the best-case scenario. And there are several reasons to be less optimistic. The AI industry shows many of the signs that it's in an unsustainable bubble. And Nvidia's business model isn't diversified enough to be cushioned against the painful impact of a spending slowdown. With these risks in mind, it looks more likely to me that when we get to the end of 2027, Nvidia shares will be trading close to flat compared to their price today. That was certainly the most powerful tailwind driving the stock higher. If Wall Street's forecast proves correct, then Nvidia's share price should mimic this bottom-line gain. That would turn a $10,000 investment in the chipmaker made today into a position worth $45,000 in three years. A 350% return in 36 months is impossible to complain about. title: OpenAI Is Buying Google’s AI Chips, a Hit to Nvidia’s Biggest Customer Bond - 24/7 Wall St.
content: OpenAI reportedly buying Google's custom AI chips would quietly shift leverage in one of the most lucrative vendor relationships in tech, and the fallout for NVIDIA's pricing power and Alphabet's chip ambitions is only beginning to take shape. OpenAI has spent more on NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) graphics processors than almost any other company, and it now plans to buy Google’s own AI chips, according to The Information. The report came out the night of October 27, 2026. It cites one person familiar with the matter and mentions Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs), custom chips built for AI work. Neither company has confirmed the plan. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and OpenAI declined to comment. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) closed at $320.58, up 1.19%, a gain of $3.78, and then added 0.93% after hours to reach $323.57. NVIDIA rose 0.9% to $217.94 and stayed nearly flat after hours at $218.14. No terms, volumes, timing, or chip generation have been disclosed. Until one of the companies confirms it, this remains a reported plan, since nobody has shown a signed order. OpenAI has used TPUs before. It began renting Google’s AI chips in June 2025, and the report adds that it now owns them. A year earlier, OpenAI said it had “no specific plans to use TPUs at present.” OpenAI has been moving in this direction for a while. It recently said it would offer its frontier models through Google Cloud. In June, it announced its first custom chip, and a current job listing asks for “significant experience optimizing real workloads on TPUs for training or inference.” A buyer this large wants a second supplier because it gains leverage on price, protection against supply shortages, and software that is not tied to a single vendor. Alphabet started selling TPUs directly to some customers this year, although its chief financial officer has said most of that revenue will be recognized in 2027. Google already rents TPUs to Anthropic, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Citadel Securities. An OpenAI purchase would show that TPUs can work as a chip business selling to outside buyers, on top of a cloud unit whose revenue grew 82% to $24.77 billion last quarter. For NVIDIA, the first measure is scale: its data center unit brought in $89.02 billion in a single quarter. Its financial ties to OpenAI are also extensive. On August 17, 2026, NVIDIA agreed to provide up to $105 billion in credit support for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that starts at 4.25 gigawatts. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang reportedly said OpenAI committed to spend about $600 billion on NVIDIA servers through 2030. OpenAI still calls itself one of NVIDIA’s biggest customers. On the same day as the report, its computing chief said, in a joint announcement with NVIDIA and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), “We are bringing Vera into production on OCI to support these workloads at scale.” Huang has said he is “very confident that they’re going to be customers and partners of ours for a very long time.” As the seller, he would naturally say that, but no evidence shows OpenAI cutting its orders. The risk to NVIDIA is a slow loss of pricing power, because each credible alternative improves the buyer’s position in negotiations. NVIDIA trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 44, and that multiple assumes NVIDIA keeps its 71.1% gross margin. TPU software still lags behind NVIDIA’s, so the purchase could be smaller or slower than the headline implies. Alphabet has fallen 5.79% over the past week and is up only 2.62% this year, while NVIDIA is up 17.13%. At a P/E of 14 and a market value of $3.874 trillion, Alphabet costs far less than NVIDIA at $5.263 trillion. That gap suggests the market gives little premium to Alphabet’s position as a credible second AI chip supplier. The next test comes when Alphabet reports after the close on October 28, 2026. If management names outside TPU buyers or raises its 2027 TPU revenue outlook, the case gets stronger. title: Nvidia Vs. Apple: Opposing Philosophies Racing Toward The Same $6 Trillion Goal - 24/7 Wall St.

Two of the world's most valuable companies are chasing the same $6 trillion milestone through opposite philosophies, and only one of them can get there first on cheaper growth. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) are worth about $5.26 trillion and $5.07 trillion. Their latest earnings reports show two opposite roads to $6 trillion. NVIDIA builds AI factories for everyone else. Apple drives AI into the over two and a half billion active devices its customers already own. NVIDIA’s fiscal second-quarter revenue reached $96.22 billion, up 105.8% YoY, and Data Center supplied $89.02 billion of it. Networking revenue rose 138%, which tells you customers now buy entire racks instead of single GPUs. CEO Jensen Huang put it simply: “Now, compute is revenue.” Is Now The Time To Buy For Alphabet, Microsoft or Nvidia? Apple posted a June-quarter record of $109.42 billion, up 16.4%. The iPhone 17 family lifted iPhone revenue 22% to $54.3 billion. Mac grew 29% as the MacBook Neo pulled schools away from Windows and Chromebooks. One caution: tariff refunds added $0.11 to Apple’s $2.02 EPS, which makes the headline look better than the underlying quarter. NVIDIA hardware runs closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic as well as open models like DeepSeek, so NVIDIA gets paid whichever model comes out ahead. title: Nvidia Stock Is 10% Below Its Record. Does Anthropic's IPO Filing Make It a Buy? - The Motley Fool
content: How much of the Claude maker's rent goes to the chip giant? Anthropic made its initial public offering (IPO) filing public on Monday, showing what the Claude maker has agreed to pay to rent computing power built on Nvidia (NVDA -0.80%) chips. Deals with three providers have a price tag: up to $120.5 billion with SpaceXAI, an arm of SpaceX (SPCX -0.92%), around $44.6 billion with Nscale, and about $41.3 billion with Lambda. All told, that's up to about $206 billion. But they're rental contracts with cloud providers, not chip orders, and the same filing commits even more money to computing on Google's chips. Nvidia shares were up about 2% on Monday as of this writing, at around $216 -- still about 10% below their Oct. 6 record close. I think the filing says less about Nvidia's future sales than that $206 billion suggests. The biggest part mainly rents capacity that's already built, or will be by December. In May, Anthropic said it would use all the capacity at SpaceX's Colossus 1 data center, which has over 220,000 Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), including older H100 and H200 chips. By late May, the deal also covered capacity at SpaceX's newer Colossus 2 site. Hardware that must be running by December is mostly already sold, or shipping now. When the full SpaceXAI capacity arrives, the rent runs around $3.1 billion a month. But those contracts are also the easiest to exit. After their initial lock-in periods end in early 2027, either side can cancel with 90 days' notice. The Nscale and Lambda deals look more like new demand, as that capacity still needs to be built. But Nscale must use its best efforts to line up financing for the Nvidia GPUs and the data center infrastructure. And Lambda's biggest agreement, around $34.9 billion, can be canceled if Lambda doesn't secure its facility lease in time. Of course, rent pays for more than chips. It also covers the buildings, the power, the financing, and the provider's profit. So Nvidia's share of the $206 billion is likely much smaller. Anthropic also committed at least $44.9 billion to Microsoft through May 2033, but didn't say how much of that runs on Nvidia chips. A July supply deal with Advanced Micro Devices for its Helios rack-scale systems could also top $20 billion if Anthropic takes its full initial capacity. Anthropic agreed to spend at least around $114.5 billion with Alphabet's (GOOGL -12.64%)(GOOG -12.29%) Google through July 2033, and it estimates that extra computing on Google's tensor processing units (TPUs) from 2028 to 2031 could cost between $125 billion and $150 billion. Its leases with Broadcom (AVGO -1.94%) for TPU-based hardware total around $161.2 billion in rent. Amazon, which makes its own Trainium chips, gets a commitment of at least $110.0 billion. Put another way, Google and Broadcom alone account for about $276 billion, leaving out the extra TPU estimate. Unlike the SpaceXAI deals, these commitments can't be canceled except in narrow cases, like a default or the other side's uncured breach. Anthropic's revenue soared to $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026 from $1.2 billion a year before. But it's steering more of its committed money to Google's chips than to Nvidia's. For the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (the three months ended July 26, 2026), Nvidia's data center business (home to its AI chips and systems) had revenue of $89.0 billion, over twice the year-ago total. That followed $75.2 billion in fiscal Q1 and $62.3 billion in fiscal Q4 2026, so the business has been adding roughly $13 billion or more every quarter. At that latest rate, the business takes in about $356 billion a year. Anthropic's full SpaceXAI rent runs about $37 billion a year, and just some of that flows to Nvidia. "This time last year, one lab alone was driving the buildout," CEO Jensen Huang said in Nvidia's fiscal Q2 earnings release. Now, he said, "multiple frontier labs" are "scaling in parallel." After all, investors aren't paying much for that growth. At around $216, Nvidia stock trades at about 14 times the earnings per share analysts expect for its fiscal 2028 (its year ending January 2028). Broadcom, in comparison, goes for about 17 times the earnings expected in its next fiscal year. So, is Nvidia stock a buy after Anthropic's filing? The $206 billion number overstates what's headed Nvidia's way, and Google's chips are winning more of Anthropic's commitments. But Nvidia's growth doesn't rest on any one lab, and its valuation arguably already assumes growth will slow sharply. I'd consider buying Nvidia stock at about $216. The filing just doesn't do much for that case by itself. Daniel Sparks and his clients do not have positions in any of the stocks mentioned. title: Nvidia’s New $3 Billion AI Bet Is on One of Its Own Customers - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia’s $3 billion investment in Meta strengthens an important partnership. It also raises familiar questions about who is funding the AI boom. Nvidia (NVDA -0.80%) announced this morning that it plans to invest $3 billion in Meta Platforms (META +1.96%), one of its biggest customers. Nvidia will make the investment as part of Meta's recently announced stock offering. The companies said they will expand their work on Muse, Meta's popular AI assistant, working to improve Meta's family of models that power it. That technical partnership aims to improve both training -- building an AI model -- and inference, using the model after it's been trained. Meta said it plans to expand its deployment of Nvidia's latest hardware: Vera Rubin GPU systems, Vera CPUs, and networking technology. The companies also said they are considering working on tools that would help AI agents operate securely as well as help monitor their behavior, but those discussions are still exploratory and nothing has been agreed upon. This is a deepening of an already close relationship. While we don't know where exactly Meta ranks, it was very likely already one of Nvidia's biggest customers, and in February, Meta said it would deploy millions of Nvidia's Blackwell and Vera Rubin GPUs, along with CPUs and networking equipment. And given the lack of detail in this announcement, it makes it a little hard to tell how much new business Nvidia is actually getting here. Meta says it will use more of its hardware, but the announcement doesn't say how much more or what those additional purchases will be worth. And their engineers were already working together, so the technical partnership sounds like an extension of work they were already doing. More than three years into the AI boom, Nvidia is still going strong. Last quarter, the company's top-line reached $96.2 billion, more than double what it recorded a year earlier. Operating profit grew a whopping 124% to $63.7 billion. It's easy to take this for granted at this point, but those really are simply incredible growth numbers for a company of this size. Unsurprisingly, Nvidia's data center business accounted for more than 90% of sales. While that is precisely what's fueling the company's rapid growth, it means Nvidia's fate is directly tied to the rest of the AI industry. Nvidia -- or rather, its stock price -- cannot afford to have the AI capex spend slow. The deal made today makes sense. Meta needs capital, and Nvidia is flush with cash. A $3 billion infusion gives Nvidia an appreciating asset -- Meta stock -- while ensuring a major customer continues to purchase its hardware. This is one of many such deals that, while completely above-board, have raised concerns over whether Nvidia is using its considerable balance sheet to paper over cracks in a less-than-healthy AI ecosystem. I think there's something to these claims, though I would caution investors to read too much into a deal like this. The reality is, Nvidia has a whole lot of cash on hand and needs to do something with it. Meta stock is a reasonable place to deploy that capital. That said, given the recent issues that hyperscalers like Meta -- and especially neoclouds like CoreWeave -- have been facing related to debt financing, it's reasonable to question how sustainable the AI buildout really is at this point. title: Nvidia Just Announced Plans to Pour Billions Into Meta's Muse - The Motley Fool
content: The chipmaker and social media titan are deepening their partnership. When Meta Platforms (META +1.96%) released its quarterly report last week, it contained more than the usual financial information. The social media and artificial intelligence (AI) purveyor announced plans to create a new class of stock -- Class C shares. This non-voting stock, which is poised to begin trading early next year, will be used primarily to raise capital for its soaring AI expenses, employee compensation, and to fund potential acquisitions. Meta plans to effect a 2-for-1 stock split on Jan. 19, 2027 -- in the form of a stock dividend -- issuing one share of Class C stock to shareholders of record for each share of Class A or Class B common stock they own. Perhaps as importantly, Meta announced plans to raise a total of $95 billion to backstop its heavy investments in AI -- and the move is attracting backing from some of the biggest names in technology. Chief among them is Nvidia (NVDA -0.80%), arguably the architect of the AI revolution. Just this morning, the semiconductor specialist announced plans to pour billions of dollars into Meta to fund its AI ambitions. In a separate press release that dropped on Monday, Nvidia and Meta announced plans to expand their collaboration on the Muse family of AI models, citing the growing popularity and demand for AI agents. Indeed, Meta's Muse models and AI agents, powered by Nvidia processors, have "delivered frontier-level benchmark performance and surging consumer downloads since launch," according to the release. The pair plan to deepen their collaboration, "by partnering on optimizations across workflows to maximize performance and improve total cost of ownership." Nvidia and Meta are also exploring other opportunities, including the use of Nvidia's OpenShell and Sentry, designed to ensure the safe deployment and monitoring of AI agent behavior. Meta also plans to increase its deployment of Nvidia's Vera Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs), Vera CPUs, and Spectrum-X Ethernet to boost the performance of its AI agents, Meta is already one of Nvidia's biggest customers. The pair expanded their partnership earlier this year, announcing a multi-year deal in which Meta would deploy "millions" of Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin chips, as well as the company's Grace and Vera CPUs. Meta's fundraising efforts will be spread out over the coming months. First, the company will raise $35 billion through an underwritten public offering, attracting foundational investors such as Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom. The trio of AI chipmakers have expressed interest in buying up to $5 billion in Meta's Class A shares, with Nvidia contributing $3 billion. Meta plans to raise another $60 billion through the sale of Class C shares beginning early next year. The fundraising binge comes at a critical time for the tech giant. Meta recently confirmed that it is on track to have 2026 capital expenditures in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion, roughly double the $72.2 billion the company spent last year. Concerns about the company's legal challenges and heavy spending on AI have weighed on Meta, which has shed 16% over the past year. However, at 21 times earnings, the stock has much of the downside potential priced in. For its part, Nvidia continues to post year-over-year revenue and profit growth of more than 100%, yet is selling for less than 28 times earnings. Despite the risk of a potential slowdown in AI-related spending, both of these industry titans are attractively priced. Danny Vena, CPA has positions in Broadcom, Meta Platforms, and Nvidia. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) announced Tuesday that it will invest $3 billion in an equity offering by Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), alongside an expansion of the companies' artificial intelligence partnership focused on Meta's Muse AI models and supporting computing infrastructure. The agreement includes collaboration on improving the training and inference performance of Meta's Muse models, as well as plans to expand the use of Nvidia hardware and networking technology across Meta's data centers. Separately, Meta increased the size of its common stock offering from $22.5 billion to $25 billion, bringing the combined potential proceeds from its common stock and depository share offerings to $37.5 billion. Under the expanded partnership, Nvidia and Meta will work together to improve the performance of Meta's Muse artificial intelligence models, including the computing processes used for model training and inference. Meta plans to increase its deployment of Nvidia infrastructure across its data centers, incorporating Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs to support its AI agents. The company also intends to deploy Nvidia networking technology as part of the infrastructure expansion. The collaboration covers both the hardware used to operate Meta's AI systems and efforts to improve the efficiency and performance of its Muse models. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the objectives of the expanded relationship in a company statement. "NVIDIA and Meta are expanding our partnership to optimize the computing infrastructure end to end for capable, efficient and secure AI agents," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. The expanded agreement follows the launch of Meta's Muse artificial intelligence models and associated AI agents. According to the announcement, the Muse agent application received a positive response from users and became one of the most downloaded applications within a week of its release. The companies intend to collaborate on further improvements to the training and inference capabilities of the Muse models. Meta's planned infrastructure expansion includes additional Nvidia computing systems and networking equipment intended to support the operation of its AI agents. Alongside the partnership announcement, Meta disclosed that it had increased the size of its common stock offering to $25 billion from the previously announced $22.5 billion. The company said the common stock offering, together with a separate depository share offering, could raise up to $37.5 billion. Meta priced the common stock issuance at $625 per share, while the depository shares were priced at $50 each. The company indicated that the proceeds are intended primarily to finance the expansion of its artificial intelligence infrastructure. Nvidia's planned $3 billion investment forms part of Meta's recent equity offering. Meta separately disclosed on Monday that it intends to undertake an additional $60 billion offering of non-voting shares in 2027. The planned transaction is distinct from the current common stock and depository share offerings. The company's announced capital-raising activities are primarily directed towards funding its AI infrastructure expansion, including the computing resources required for its artificial intelligence models and agents. The proposed 2027 offering remains a future financing plan, while the current offerings have been priced at $625 per common share and $50 per depository share. title: NVIDIA and Meta to Expand Collaboration on Muse and Muse Family of Models Amid Robust Growth - NVIDIA Newsroom
content:
NVIDIA and Meta today announced they will partner to expand their work on Muse and the Muse family of models to improve inference and training performance, reflecting popular demand for useful AI agents. Meta’s Muse models and agents, which leverage NVIDIA’s infrastructure, have delivered frontier-level benchmark performance and surging consumer downloads since launch. Meta and NVIDIA intend to further deepen their collaboration by partnering on optimizations across workflows to maximize performance and improve total cost of ownership. Meta and NVIDIA will also consider additional collaboration opportunities with NVIDIA on its NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, including NVIDIA OpenShell™ for safe deployment and NVIDIA Sentry for monitoring agent behavior. This announcement reinforces Meta and NVIDIA’s strong long-term partnership to support Meta’s AI infrastructure ambitions. Meta intends to expand the deployment of NVIDIA infrastructure, including Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs for next-generation AI agents to deliver maximum performance per watt. Meta will also deploy NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ Ethernet networking and BlueField-4® to support network efficiency and throughput. In addition, NVIDIA will invest $3 billion in Meta’s equity offering. “AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents. NVIDIA and Meta are expanding our partnership to optimize the computing infrastructure end to end for capable, efficient and secure AI agents, so Muse can empower billions of people to achieve more and pursue greater ambitions.” “Muse is how we bring personal superintelligence to everyone. We’re excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people,” said Mark Zuckerberg, founder and CEO of Meta. About NVIDIA

ImmunityBio (IBRX) shares rose nearly 1% overnight heading into Tuesday after CNBC host Jim Cramer called it a “very good spec,” citing a wave of biotech acquisitions as the company advances plans to expand the use of its flagship drug, Anktiva, in bladder cancer. IBRX stock closed Monday down about 5% at $7.81, logging its fourth straight session in the red. Cramer backed ImmunityBio as a speculative bet during Monday’s Mad Money Lightning Round, saying it could pay off even when index funds disappoint. “I don’t mind you taking a position in that, because that’s one of those that you could look back and say, you know what? I was in my index funds, they didn’t really do well, but man, did I clean up on a very good spec,” he said. He pointed to biotech takeovers as part of the appeal. “The biotechs are being taken over like mad, you want to be in one,” Cramer said. The call echoes his June stance, when he encouraged investors to limit speculation to one holding. “Let Immunitybio be your speculation,” he said then. Cramer’s takeover pitch follows a string of recent big drugmaker deals. Earlier this month, Viatris agreed to buy Pacira BioSciences for $1.65 billion, with closing expected by year-end. AbbVie completed its $10.9 billion acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics in September, while Eli Lilly agreed in August to acquire Merida Biosciences for up to $2.875 billion, including milestone payments. Cramer’s backing comes ahead of a November readout that could help ImmunityBio bring Anktiva to patients earlier in bladder cancer treatment. Last week, the company finished checking data from a 366-patient trial comparing Anktiva plus BCG with BCG alone in non-muscle invasive bladder cancer, clearing the way for the final analysis. The study focuses on patients receiving BCG-based treatment for the first time. Anktiva’s current approval covers patients whose disease has not responded to BCG. ImmunityBio also plans to submit an application to expand FDA approval in the fourth quarter. The analysis will assess how many patients achieve a complete response, meaning no detectable cancer under the study’s criteria, and how long those responses last. Earlier this month, the FDA expanded ANKTIVA plus BCG’s approval to include patients with BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer with papillary-only tumors. That builds on its 2024 approval for disease with carcinoma in situ, with or without papillary tumors. The company also released long-term results this month from a Phase 2/3 study of 100 patients whose cancer had not responded to BCG. It reported a 71% complete response rate, with some responses lasting more than 53 months. Among responders, three-year survival without bladder-removal surgery was 84%. title: Nvidia NVDA Stock Rebounds on Chip Sentiment Improving but Data-Centre Risks Remain - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia stock rebounded from $210 as semiconductor sentiment improved, but data-centre power shortages, expensive financing, manufacturing constraints and growing competition raise questions about whether infrastructure spending can sustain demand for advanced processors. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares recovered above $215 after touching $210 last Friday, regaining some ground following a retreat from a record above $243 earlier this month. The rebound reflects renewed buying interest across the semiconductor sector, supported by expectations that memory shortages and higher prices could persist through 2027. However, the recovery comes as investors increasingly question the financial returns from expanding computing infrastructure. Rising borrowing costs, expensive equipment and electricity constraints are complicating the expansion plans of major technology companies. Nvidia remains a leading supplier of advanced processors, but its growth increasingly depends on customers having the financial resources, electricity and infrastructure required to deploy the hardware they purchase. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) is reportedly purchasing billions of dollars in Nvidia hardware, yet some server racks are sitting in warehouses because data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them, according to Business Insider. Internal emails reportedly indicated that Amazon expected to receive $5 billion in Nvidia server systems in August, followed by another $3 billion monthly. The company also introduced an Early Rack Receipt programme, allowing it to secure equipment before facilities are ready for deployment. Previously, Amazon generally waited until hardware reached its data centres before taking ownership. The revised arrangement helps secure scarce equipment but also exposes the company to storage costs and delays between delivery and commercial use. For Nvidia, this highlights a potential weakness in the infrastructure expansion cycle. Strong orders may support near-term demand, but delayed deployments could postpone returns for customers and influence future purchasing decisions. If electricity shortages persist, technology companies may reconsider the timing and scale of new projects, particularly as infrastructure costs rise. Expectations for higher memory prices have provided some support to semiconductor shares. Dell CEO Michael Dell reportedly warned that memory shortages could worsen in 2027, while analysts at Mizuho and KeyBanc have highlighted the potential for NAND flash prices to increase as demand for computing infrastructure expands. Higher memory prices could benefit manufacturers across the supply chain, but they also increase the cost of building and operating data centres. For Nvidia, the key question is whether customers can maintain their investment plans while absorbing rising expenses for processors, memory, electricity and construction. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $210 again last week but we’re seeing some improvement this week. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that planned semiconductor manufacturing capacity in 2027 and 2028 might not fully meet anticipated demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Despite these figures, its U.S.-listed shares reportedly fell approximately 4%, adding pressure to Nvidia and AMD. Manufacturing constraints could support semiconductor pricing, but they may also delay the equipment needed to expand production. This creates a difficult balance for the industry: demand remains strong, yet supply limitations could restrict growth. Financing concerns have intensified following heavy selling in CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV). Yields on its $1.25 billion bond issue due in 2032 reportedly reached 15% before closing near 14.5%, signalling substantial investor concern about credit risk. Such borrowing costs raise questions about the sustainability of debt-financed data-centre expansion. If infrastructure operators face increasingly expensive financing, some projects could be delayed or scaled back, weakening future demand for Nvidia processors. Reported financing discussions involving major technology companies further illustrate the substantial capital required to sustain the industry’s expansion. Microsoft’s Maia 300 processor adds another competitive risk. The chip reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while a 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of its predecessor. Custom silicon could help cloud providers improve efficiency and reduce dependence on external suppliers for selected workloads. Nvidia’s established software ecosystem and broad customer base remain important advantages, but increasingly capable alternatives could eventually pressure its pricing power and market share in specific applications. Questions about OpenAI’s revenue have renewed scrutiny of technology-sector spending assumptions. Its annualised revenue run rate was reportedly around $50 billion at the end of September, below the widely circulated $68 billion figure, which reportedly included revenue generated by partners. The distinction matters because investors need evidence that the commercial demand supporting infrastructure investment can justify its enormous costs. If revenue growth fails to keep pace with spending, technology companies could face pressure to reduce capital expenditure, potentially affecting future processor orders. Nvidia’s rebound above $215 provides some relief after the retreat from $243, but the recovery remains vulnerable to renewed selling. The ability to sustain gains will depend partly on whether major customers can overcome electricity constraints, secure financing and generate sufficient returns from their infrastructure investments. For now, memory shortages and continued demand for advanced processors support the bullish case. However, rising financing costs, manufacturing bottlenecks and competition from custom chips create significant risks. Nvidia’s long-term growth prospects remain substantial, but the sustainability of its rally increasingly depends on whether customers can turn expensive computing infrastructure into profitable businesses.
